questions.stem: On a telemetry unit, frequent nonactionable alarms have led staff to silence alarms reflexively, and a true lethal arrhythmia alarm was recently missed. Which systems response best addresses this hazard?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Reduce alarm volume across the unit during high-noise periods and rely more heavily on visual displays so repeated alerts are less disruptive to staff workflow overall.","B":"Disable repeated alarms after the first notification because a previously acknowledged alarm no longer needs to remain audible if the condition continues.","C":"Individualize alarm limits when clinically appropriate, reduce nonactionable alarms through policy, and ensure actionable alarms remain audible and promptly addressed.","D":"Use the same default alarm limits for clients on the unit because standardization is more important than tailoring thresholds to the monitored condition."}}
questions.rationale: Alarm-safety programs should reduce unnecessary/nonactionable alarm burden without suppressing clinically important alarms. Settings should be clinically appropriate, actionable alarms must remain detectable, and staff response processes must prevent desensitization and delayed recognition of true emergencies.
questions.source_name: FDA — Human Factors Considerations for Medical Devices and Alarm Safety
questions.source_detail: FDA human-factors guidance recognizes that alarm noise and poorly designed alarm management can impair detection and response to clinically important signals.

questions.stem: A client on Contact Precautions for a multidrug-resistant organism is discharged. Before a high-risk client is admitted to the same room, what environmental action is appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Change the bed linens and leave reusable equipment in the room because standard detergent cleaning is sufficient once the colonized client has departed.","B":"Clean visibly soiled surfaces and high-touch areas, but leave low-touch surfaces for scheduled cleaning because the patient has already left the room.","C":"Move shared equipment directly to the next room after wiping handles with water because terminal cleaning applies to the room but not to noncritical equipment.","D":"Perform terminal cleaning and disinfection of the room and reprocess reusable equipment according to facility procedures before admitting the next client."}}
questions.rationale: CDC terminal/discharge cleaning includes cleaning and disinfection of high- and low-touch surfaces and reprocessing reusable noncritical patient-care equipment before the next patient occupies the space. Linen change or visible-surface cleaning alone is insufficient.
questions.source_detail: CDC terminal cleaning after discharge/transfer includes cleaning and disinfecting the patient-care area and reprocessing reusable noncritical equipment.

questions.stem: A nurse assigned to care for patients requiring N95 respiratory protection was last fit-tested 14 months ago and has had no facial changes. What is required before continued use?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Complete another fit test because a tight-fitting respirator requires fit testing before initial use, after a facepiece change, and at least annually thereafter.","B":"Continue with the existing fit test because annual retesting is unnecessary when the same respirator model and size are used and facial features have not changed.","C":"Replace fit testing with a user seal check because a successful seal check at each use satisfies the OSHA requirement for periodic respirator fit testing.","D":"Repeat the medical evaluation instead of fit testing because periodic medical clearance is the requirement that determines continued respirator use."}}
questions.rationale: OSHA requires fit testing for tight-fitting respirators before initial use, whenever a different facepiece is used, and at least annually thereafter. Additional fit testing is required when physical changes could affect fit; a user seal check does not replace required fit testing.
questions.source_detail: 29 CFR 1910.134(f): fit testing before initial use, when a different facepiece is used, and at least annually thereafter; additional testing for physical changes affecting fit.

questions.stem: During a mass-casualty incident using the START adult triage algorithm, an adult victim remains apneic after the airway is repositioned. How is this victim categorized in START?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Red/immediate, because any victim with an airway problem receives the highest transport priority even when breathing does not resume after airway repositioning.","B":"Black/expectant under the START algorithm, because absence of spontaneous breathing after airway repositioning does not meet criteria for the immediate category.","C":"Yellow/delayed, because the absence of breathing indicates severe injury but allows transport to be postponed while victims with circulation problems are treated first.","D":"Green/minor, because respiratory categorization occurs after ambulatory victims have been separated and the victim can be reassessed during transport."}}
questions.rationale: In the START adult triage algorithm, an apneic victim whose breathing does not resume after airway repositioning is categorized black/expectant. The algorithm is a disaster-triage allocation tool and differs from routine single-patient resuscitation.
questions.source_name: HHS REMM — START Adult Triage Algorithm
questions.source_detail: START adult triage uses respiratory status first; no spontaneous breathing after airway repositioning leads to the black/expectant category.

questions.stem: A nurse accidentally emails unsecured PHI to the wrong recipient, who confirms opening and reading it. What should the nurse do next?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Delete the sent message from the nurse's mailbox and take no further action because removing the local copy eliminates the privacy risk created by the disclosure.","B":"Send an individual breach notice and report directly to HHS before the privacy office evaluates whether an exception or low-probability-of-compromise determination applies.","C":"Ask the recipient to keep the information confidential and close the incident because voluntary cooperation removes the disclosure from HIPAA breach requirements.","D":"Report the incident promptly through the organization's privacy process so mitigation, breach-risk assessment, and required notifications can be completed safely."}}
questions.rationale: An impermissible disclosure of unsecured PHI is presumed to be a breach unless the covered entity demonstrates a low probability of compromise using the required risk assessment. The workforce member should promptly report the incident through the organization's privacy process so mitigation, risk assessment, and any required individual/HHS notifications can occur.
questions.source_detail: Impermissible unsecured-PHI disclosures require breach risk assessment and, when applicable, notification; current HHS guidance also specifies reporting obligations and timelines.
